slides.title: Signed-out Session lifecycle
slides.subtitle: Start a Session with no network call, sign every request, restart once when refused
slides.notes: Every interaction a personal agent has with a company happens inside a Session. A Session is local: the agent makes it, with a random sid, and asks the company nothing. This example starts one signed out, sends requests in it, and shows what happens when the company answers invalid_session.

slides.title: Why start signed out
slides.statement: The company recognises the **same user** across visits, without learning **who** they are.
slides.notes: A signed-out Session gives the company a stable, pairwise context: the same User ID every time this agent comes back for this user, and a different one at every other company. Public questions and a conversation can start here, and continue later through sign-in.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB H["PAP host
holds the PapSession"] -- "sign this request" --> S["Reactor Session signer
one delegated key per User ID"] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB A["Company API
verifies the Session header"] end HOST -- "request, Poppy-Session" --> CO CO -- "answer or invalid_session" --> HOST HOST -. "status only" .-> M
slides.caption: The keys live in a replaceable Reactor contribution; the model sees the Session's status, never its ID.
slides.notes: Inside your trusted host, the PAP host holds the PapSession and asks the Reactor Session signer for a Session JWT for each request. The signer keeps one delegated key per User ID, and a delegation that vouches for it. The JWT crosses to the company in the Poppy-Session header, and the company verifies it before anything else. It answers, or refuses with invalid_session. Off to the side, the model receives the lifecycle status, nothing it could leak.

items.title: Met
items.detail: An unknown `sid` starts a signed-out Session

slides.notes: SessionClient.start makes a PapSession with a random sid. There is no grant and no token. The company first hears of the Session on the first request: it verifies the Session header, sees a sid it does not know, and starts a signed-out Session for that client_id and User ID.

slides.title: Every later request

items.title: Sign again
items.detail: A new JWT: a new `jti`, this method and URL

items.title: Same `sid`
items.detail: The company continues the same Session

items.title: Signed in, if a token goes with it
items.detail: On each request that carries an access token

slides.notes: A Session JWT covers one request, so each request signs a new one. The sid stays the same, and that is what continues the Session. A Session is signed in on each request that carries an access token, and signed out on each that does not. Sign-in itself does not know the Session.

slides.title: The whole exchange
slides.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as PAP host
  participant C as Company
  H->>H: Start: a random sid
  H->>C: Request, Poppy-Session
  C-->>H: Answer
  H->>C: Next request, a fresh JWT, same sid
  C-->>H: 400 invalid_session
  H->>H: A new sid, once
  H->>C: The same request, in the new Session
  C-->>H: Answer
  H->>C: Next request
  C-->>H: 400 invalid_session
  H->>H: A new sid
  H->>C: The same request
  C-->>H: 400 invalid_session
  H->>H: Stop: the caller gets the refusal
slides.notes: Here is the whole exchange at once. The first request starts the Session at the company. Later a request draws invalid_session: the Session failed a check, or it has ended. The client makes a new sid and sends the request again in the new Session, and it goes through. In the example a later request is refused, and so is its one resend. A second invalid_session in a row is not retried: it goes back to the caller.

slides.title: Restart once, then stop
slides.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Signed out" as SO
  state "Signed in, on this request" as SI
  state "Refused" as R
  state "Stopped" as X
  [*] --> SO : start, no network call
  SO --> SI : an access token goes with it
  SI --> SO : no access token
  SO --> R : invalid_session
  SI --> R : invalid_session
  R --> SO : a new sid, the request sent again
  R --> X : invalid_session again
  X --> [*]
slides.caption: A restart keeps the User ID and changes the sid; a second refusal stops the client.
slides.notes: Start at the dot: the host starts the Session signed out, with no network call. A request with an access token is signed in; one without is signed out. invalid_session can come in either. The client then makes a new sid, keeps the same User ID and delegated key, and sends the request again. If that is refused too, it stops. To end a Session without signing out, the agent simply stops using its sid; its refresh tokens are unaffected.

slides.title: What stays where

left.heading: Host-owned, never the model's
items: Session IDs and pairwise User IDs

slides.notes: None of the credentials reach the model. Session IDs, User IDs, Session JWTs, delegations and keys stay in host code and protected storage; the model sees the Session's status and nothing it could leak.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples run this lifecycle against a deterministic company
slides.notes: The example's company answers invalid_session on chosen requests, so the restart is exercised on every run. Production code uses the same SessionClient and SessionHttpClient over real HTTPS, with managed Reactor contributions.
